articles.title: Nations Championship: England will not get carried away by win against All Blacks - Matt Dawson
articles.summary: In his latest BBC Sport column, England World Cup winner Matt Dawson reflects on Steve Borthwick's side's record win over New Zealand and previews the final round of Nations Championship fixtures.
articles.body:
In his latest BBC Sport column, England World Cup winner Matt Dawson reflects on Steve Borthwick's side's record win over New Zealand and previews the final round of Nations Championship fixtures.

If England had produced that performance two years ago against New Zealand, there would have been a lap of honour and wild celebrations.

Saturday felt like business. Job done, move on. And that is how it should be.

It was a record victory for a northern hemisphere side against the All Blacks, yet at full-time you would hardly have known it.

Even the post-match messaging from their leaders - Maro Itoje, Ellis Genge and Steve Borthwick - was that this performance had always been in them and that nobody was surprised.

A tired but hurting New Zealand side will arrive at Allianz Stadium next Saturday looking for revenge.

England beat the All Blacks in back-to-back Tests in 2002 and 2003. Matching that achievement on Saturday was a significant statement.

Three consecutive wins over New Zealand, followed by a third-place finish, would leave England in a strong position heading into 2027, when the Rugby World Cup takes place in Australia.

Lose, though, and it will be a waste of some great momentum.

We have had many a false dawn with Borthwick's England, but something feels different this time.

For me, that comes down to the players taking responsibility.

Many of us ex-pros called for it during the Six Nations, and finally we are seeing the players take the lead on the style of rugby they want to play.

It is an exciting, free-flowing brand of attacking rugby that mirrors what they are used to playing in the Prem.

England's backs can compete with the very best and they tore through New Zealand on multiple occasions.

Credit also has to go to Borthwick for allowing the players to take control. That, in itself, shows how he is learning and evolving as a head coach.

Once players start getting 40, 50, 60 or 70 caps, they know more about certain aspects of the game than the coach because they are the ones out there experiencing it.

If the environment does not allow players to turn around and say 'this isn't going to work', then it is never going to work.

The reports before the Australia game suggested honest conversations took place, with the players wanting a greater say in how the team operates.

The Six Nations was probably a big turning point. The change in mood and the feel-good factor are clear in the way England are carrying themselves.

They now feel in control and, crucially, have a genuine sense of ownership in shaping the team and how it plays.

'An enormous statement about English rugby'

Lewis Moody, a former team-mate of mine, joining the team to face the New Zealand haka was an enormous statement about English rugby.

Whether you are playing in 2026 or 1926, this is England rugby. We are together.

It was a united and extraordinary moment, one that will stay with me until the day I die. There was a clear bond as Lewis embraced every England player before leaving the pitch.

That was a huge driver for England. They were able to show their emotional vulnerability before quickly switching into game mode.

A record victory over New Zealand was so fitting for the occasion, but I am not getting overly carried away by the big scoreline.

The southern hemisphere teams are coming towards the end of a brutally long season. They have done a lot of travelling and played considerably more international rugby.

New Zealand and South Africa, in particular, had the added emotion of four summer Tests against each other in the 'Rugby's Greatest Rivalry' series.

The Springboks also looked tired and strangely out of sorts in their defeat by Ireland.

At the beginning of the tournament, we were probably looking at it thinking it was a shame that the two top teams in the world were going to be on the same side of the draw.

Now, they have both lost back-to-back games, with injuries also playing a part.

England should not get carried away, by any stretch. It will be incredibly difficult for New Zealand to pick themselves up after that defeat.

The flight is waiting to take them home, they need some rest and will want to start thinking about next year's World Cup.

England, by contrast, will be chomping at the bit. They have momentum, and everybody is itching to get the white shirt on and run out at Allianz Stadium.

Saturday will provide another really good test of how England deal with being favourites. I expect changes to be made, but I still expect England to win.

After some difficult moments during this World Cup cycle, we are now seeing proper depth start to come through.

I can name at least two quality options in every position.

Can win over All Blacks finally break England's boom-bust cycle?

Rugby Union Weekly: England eclipse the All Blacks after record-breaking win

Ex-captain Moody joins England in emotional haka response

France will probably go into the final as favourites against South Africa.

Closing out back-to-back Six Nations titles and last week's victory over the world champions has given them the confidence to believe they can secure further silverware.

The Nations Championship has been a big success in replicating tournament rugby and, crucially, teaching teams how to win tight games.

Never write off the Springboks, but France are flying high after their performances against Argentina and South Africa.

Rassie Erasmus' side have lost back-to-back games, ending any perceived sense of invincibility. However, they only needed a point to reach the final and got that in Dublin.

Now it is winner takes all, and the world champions - with back-to-back Rugby World Cups and Rugby Championships behind them - should be in their element.

Fabien Galthie has rotated his squad tremendously well, and France will have more energy heading into next Sunday's final.

Those two points gained away to New Zealand with a second-string team in July ultimately proved decisive in the final standings.

I would have loved England to be competing for a trophy on this final weekend, but France have been the more consistent side.

The tables have turned, and suddenly the top teams in the world are in the northern hemisphere.

That is the magic of this new tournament. Everything can change in the space of a week.

Matt Dawson was speaking to BBC Sport's Alastair Telfer.

articles.title: Wales show signs of progress despite defeat by Australia, say Scrum V pundits
articles.summary: Wales believe they are on the up despite failing to back up their win against New Zealand when beaten by Australia in the Nations Championship.
articles.body:
For experienced hooker Ryan Elias, the proof of Wales' progress came when he looked around in the post-match huddle and saw heads down after a narrow defeat by Australia.

Steve Tandy's side failed to back up their historic victory against New Zealand when edged out 29-26 by the Wallabies in the Nations Championship.

Wales could not claim another scalp against the Aussies, who are two places above them in seventh in World Rugby's rankings, but they went close.

"It wasn't that long ago, not even 12 months ago, that we probably would have been chuffed with that result," said 54-cap forward Elias.

"You look around the circle at the end of that game and there were boys with heads down because this is one that got away.

"That just shows the growth of the group and the belief that's coming."

Wales coach Tandy frustrated by Australia defeat

Wales should have picked Botham, says flanker's dad

Next Sunday is the one-year anniversary of Wales' 73-0 defeat by South Africa in Cardiff, a hammering that was followed by heavy Six Nations losses against England and France.

Tandy's squad have since enjoyed victories against Italy, Fiji and Japan before the statement success against New Zealand.

"It's hard to recreate what they did against the All Blacks," former Wales centre Tom Shanklin said on Scrum V podcast.

"It's hard to get to that level every week, but it was really positive. We're still in a building phase.

"We said the best thing about the Japan game was that it was a bonus-point win, and that was about it.

"That feels a long time ago. We've come a long, long way.

"The effort was there against Australia, but there just wasn't that clinical edge and maybe that's a psychological thing."

Wales were nervy 28-21 winners at the start of November against a Japan side who have since been thumped by England and Scotland.

They face the Brave Blossoms again on Saturday (13:10 GMT) at Nations Championship finals weekend at Allianz Stadium in Twickenham.

"This is a big game now to see how much we've changed and developed from the first game of the campaign to the last," said Shanklin.

Wales chalked up four-try bonuses in all three games in Cardiff and have added to their threat from driving line-out.

They have profited from consistency at 10-12-13 with Sam Costelow, Max Llewellyn and Eddie James.

"You're seeing a team that seems to have found an attack," said Shanklin.

"Matt Sherratt has worked really hard with them and we've got various options now, we're not too predictable.

"We're playing with a lot more quick ball and we're quite clever in how we're breaking teams down.

"There are multiple options now when taking the ball to the line and we are getting it into the hands of our strike runners."

Wales did, however, waste a number of 22 entries in the first half and the final try by Ryan Elias came after pressure that ate into the clock.

"We were really good up to about five or 10 metres out, then we lost the detail," said former Wales and Lions wing Alex Cuthbert on Scrum V.

"We didn't do a lot to get held up over the line. We were quite predictable around the corner and Australia won every physical battle and were very good defensively."

Louis Rees-Zammit vowed in the summer that he would fire during his second season back in rugby after his crack at the NFL.

The 6ft 2in wing has been true to his word and arguably the 2021 Lions tourist is a better player now than he was before heading to America in 2024.

Rees-Zammit provided more evidence of his pace and added power when creating Blair Murray's try down the right in the second half.

"I was in line with where Zam had the ball and thought that surely Harry Potter was not going to give him the outside," said Cuthbert.

"It was only three or four yards and he did a shimmy in and if he gets half a yard outside then he is so quick.

"But now he is so strong from the hip down, so broke through Potter and then [Joseph-Aukuso] Suaalii tried to come across and it looked like they got an arm on him.

"It's just that power and watch Rees-Zammit carry now and he makes yard after contact."

The Bristol back has returned to wing and Murray, one of Wales' star performers in 2024-25, has profited from starting at full-back.

"He's a class player isn't he?" said the Scarlets man about Rees-Zammit. "He is one of the best wingers in the world, and he shows it week in and week out.

"We're working well together, you know. Whether I'm putting him through holes or he's getting through and passing it back inside.

"That connection is growing and we want to get the ball in our hands as much as we can."

The pair and experienced wing Josh Adams look sure to start the Six Nations, fitness permitting.

Tandy opted to change a winning team, going back to the starters that faced Japan.

His decision to rest flanker James Botham is in the spotlight after his man-of-the-match display against the All Blacks.

Alex Mann was to the fore in a different way despite suffering a painful early poke in the eye from team-mate Ben Carter, coming up with a turnover, claiming five line-outs and riling the Wallabies.

"You're certainly looking at the squad now thinking you're a lot more confident if there are injuries," said Shanklin.

"To have strength and depth with two quality players in every single position then you have got to play them.

"You cannot just have your first team out every game, then when players come in they are not going to be up to that level or have that experience. You've got to mix and match a bit."

Tandy is poised to rotate his squad for Saturday's fixture against Japan, when Wales travel to London after three games on home soil.

It will be the first game of a double-header on the day, and a warm-up for England's rematch with New Zealand.

Wales' win against the All Blacks gave a boost to ticket sales for the Wallabies fixture despite the late kick-off time.

The crowd of 66,307 was larger than the 52,425 against Japan and 55,152 against New Zealand.

Crucially, after the lows of last season's heavy defeats by South Africa and France, the connection seems strong between Tandy's team and the supporters.

"The atmosphere was amazing again," said Cuthbert, who scored two tries in the bedlam of the famous 2013 victory against England.

"You've got to give credit to the Principality Stadium staff, they are really making the place have that bit of theatre and entertainment."

Wales will hope it gives them an extra lift for the visits of Ireland and England in the Six Nations.

Image caption, Alex Mann started every game in the 2026 Six Nations
Image caption, Wales will play two home games in the 2027 Six Nations

articles.title: Wales v Japan: Steve Tandy set for Nations Championship play-off changes
articles.summary: The choices facing Steve Tandy as the Wales head coach gets set to rotate his side for the Nations Championship finale against Japan.
articles.body:
Wales head coach Steve Tandy, with one eye on the World Cup, vowed to rotate his side for Nations Championship finals weekend even before his side had faced Australia.

Hopes of an autumn clean sweep - something only achieved once in 2018 under Warren Gatland - were dashed by the Wallabies at the Principality Stadium on Saturday.

Wales dust themselves down before finishing the November campaign against familiar foes Japan on Saturday (13:10 GMT).

The Six Nations is not a time for experimenting, so it presents a rare chance to have a look at players in the countdown to next year's World Cup in Australia.

Wales spluttered to victory against Eddie Jones' side at the start of the month and will expect a more comfortable success at Twickenham's Allianz Stadium.

The fixture, a fifth meeting with the Brave Blossoms in 16 months, presents a chance for Tandy to test his squad depth.

Did beaten Wales still show they have come a long way?

Wales coach Tandy frustrated by Australia defeat

Eleven of Wales' players started against Japan, New Zealand and Australia - Blair Murray, Louis Rees-Zammit, Eddie James, Max Llewellyn, Sam Costelow, Tomos Williams, Nicky Smith, Dewi Lake, Archie Griffin, Dafydd Jenkins and Jac Morgan.

It is fair to assume that plenty of big hitters will watch from the stands at Twickenham, after the mental and physical demands of the past fortnight.

"I can rotate the team and we'll still put in a performance. It doesn't matter who wears the shirt, we've got to perform," said Tandy.

"Whenever we put a team out, the objective is to win a Test match. That will be no different next Saturday."

The core of the first-choice team will remain in England after the Japan game and rejoin their clubs in the Prem.

Former Wales and Lions wing Alex Cuthbert urged Tandy to resist the temptation to give the frontline players a breather.

"We need to put our best team out. We really want to put a marker down against Japan," he said on the Scrum V podcast.

"It's an opportunity to really put Japan to the sword if we really want to take some momentum into the Six Nations."

The Japanese are stretched by injury and conceded 24 tries in defeats by England and Scotland.

Wales fielded the same starting line-up against Japan and Australia either side of the New Zealand victory.

Man of the match against the All Blacks James Botham went from the XV to missing out completely against the Wallabies, much to the frustration of his father Liam.

Botham's fellow Cardiff back-row forward Taine Basham and Leicester wing Gabriel Hamer-Webb suffered the same fate.

Versatile forward Taine Plumtree has proved his worth from the bench in the past two fixtures but might hope for a first Test start since Scotland in the third round of the 2026 Six Nations.

Tandy is spoilt for choice in the back-row and gave promising Exeter flanker Kane James a second cap off the bench against the Wallabies.

Wales have also developed depth at loose-head prop to the extent that strong-running Rhys Carre, Welsh Rugby Writers' Association (WRWA) player of the year after his Six Nations exploits, missed out against New Zealand and Australia.

Smith has started all three November Tests and Ospreys' Gareth Thomas has been strong off the bench.

Wales selected three uncapped players in their initial Nations Championship squad with Cardiff loose-head prop Rhys Barratt, who played against the Barbarians in the summer, joined by the Dragons pair of scrum-half Che Hope and centre Aneurin Owen.

That figure became four when in-form Scarlets wing Macs Page got a call-up due to Rio Dyer's hamstring injury.

Tandy has given first caps to nine players since taking the reins in the summer of 2025 and could hit double figures at Twickenham.

There are seven other players in the squad who are yet to feature this month.

Centre Joe Hawkins failed to get off the bench against the Wallabies, when he was also Costelow's cover at fly-half.

Hooker Liam Belcher, tight-head Keiron Assiratti, lock Seb Davies, wing Ellis Mee and wing or full-back Tom Rogers have had no minutes, while fly-half Jarrod Evans was called into the squad last week when Dan Edwards suffered an injury in training.

Reuben Morgan-Williams scored a sniping try in the win against the Barbarians in June.

The Ospreys scrum-half will hope to wear nine on his back for the first time in a Test match on the return to Twickenham.

Wales have been reliant on world-class Tomos Williams, and his deputy Kieran Hardy faces a fitness race for the World Cup after a serious knee injury.

Morgan-Williams was called into the fray for the last quarter of an hour against New Zealand and was introduced just five minutes into the second half against the Wallabies.

"Reuben played a fair part of the game and did really well," said Tandy. "He was very accurate in what he did.

"Tomos had a tight groin and we will assess that, but we've got to find out about Reuben."

Wales are scheduled to name their team on Thursday morning.

images.caption: Image caption, Prop Rhys Carre came off the bench for Wales against Japan in Cardiff
Image caption, Reuben Morgan-Williams kicked the ball off to seal victory for Wales against New Zealand

articles.title: Ireland 20-17 South Africa: Andy Farrell says Springboks win 'sets us up nicely'
articles.summary: Ireland head coach Andy Farrell says his side's victory over South Africa "sets us up nicely" for the the countdown to next year's World Cup.
articles.body:
After Ireland's win over world champions South Africa on Saturday, Andy Farrell had one eye on the past, and another on what is to come.

It was a result that had left Ireland's head coach brimming with pride, as they ended a run of six straight defeats against either the Springboks, New Zealand or France.

With the World Cup now just 10 months away, it is all part of the bigger picture as Ireland aim to progress past the quarter-finals for the first time, with the ultimate goal of lifting the Webb Ellis Cup.

"Whether we lose by three or win by three, you understand how you apply yourself in a big game like that, and it doesn't get any bigger," Farrell said after the 20-17 win.

"You're always trying to kick on to the next level, and sometimes you don't know what that level is because you've never been there as a group.

"But this group is like that. We're trying to do new things together, and it sets us up nicely to keep kicking on."

Farrell looked back to the opening three matches of the Nations Championship in July, when he handed a number of players minutes at international level against Australia and Japan - such as Nick Timoney, Tom Stewart and Tom Clarkson.

Those players played a key role in downing the Springboks in Dublin as second-half replacements.

"We chose to take players to the Southern Hemisphere who had not had that type of experience.

"It's never going to be smelling of roses in that regard [performances over 80 minutes], so you end up where you're at, but we grew as a group, so therefore it's priceless for us."

Did Springboks win change the narrative for Ireland?

Ireland remind themselves that the best are beatable

Ireland beat the Boks: Post-match reaction with Josh Van der Flier and Mike McCarthy

Given how the tables were weighted, Ireland would have topped the southern hemisphere table by two points.

But the northern hemisphere's domination of the inaugural competition meant a more condensed table, and a fifth-place play-off against Australia will be their reward.

But Friday will be another tough test against a Wallabies side who were one missed penalty away from beating Ireland in Sydney in July.

Speaking before he knew who Ireland would be playing, and when, Farrell denied that playing for fifth place would be an anti-climax.

"You can only deal with what's in front of you," he said.

"We've got another week of international rugby together. We're in the green shirt, and that's special and it's a privilege, so we'll look forward to that."

Ireland's team selection to face South Africa had a surprise as captain Dan Sheehan, who usually plays at hooker, was named to start at number eight.

It was only his second professional start in the back row, with his first outing coming for Leinster against Munster before the international window.

Farrell's decision was certainly justified as Sheehan more than played his role in a scrum that held its own against the world-leading Springbok pack.

"He's so calm, isn't he? I spoke to him over the last couple of weeks about all sorts of things, about number eight, but he wasn't worried and it doesn't bother him in the slightest," said Farrell.

"It's like, 'why are you asking me that question?'. It's almost like an insult. He's so calm, he's such a gifted rugby player.

"That's his character. He just sees it for what it is and he gets on with it. That calm and influence has a knock-on effect that goes through the team."

Another standout for Ireland was Jamison Gibson-Park, whose experience and guile helped the hosts get over the line as the Boks piled on late pressure.

One clearing kick, from his own try line to the halfway line, was a particular standout in a game filled with classy moments.

Farrell described the 34-year-old's kicking as "immense", and said he is getting better with each passing year.

"He got us out of trouble so many times. You almost expect it from him, but you shouldn't," said Farrell.

"He is growing the whole time. I've never seen him in this good of nick, it just shows the hunger that he's got.

"That's what we've got within our group as well, we've got senior players who are constantly working so hard to continue to get better."

images.caption: Image caption, Andy Farrell's Ireland beat South Africa on Saturday

articles.title: Nations Championship: Rassie Erasmus set to host France watch-along as South Africa coaches deny contact during Ireland loss
articles.summary: South Africa coaches have denied contact with suspended head coach Rassie Erasmus during their 20-17 Nations Championship defeat to Ireland in Dublin; Erasmus streamed a live watch-along in which he could have breached team rules by communicating with staff or criticising officials
articles.body:
Erasmus was barred from having any involvement in matchday activity as part of a six-game ban from World Rugby for questioning whether "match-fixing" and "manipulation" was occurring in rugby after his side's thrilling defeat to France in Paris .

The 54-year-old nevertheless hosted the watch-along from the team's hotel, where he was muted for large spells of the event but could be seen speaking to an unknown party while wearing earbuds and covering his mouth.

The head coach has now announced that he will host another watch-along for South Africa's Nations Championship final clash against France at Twickenham on Sunday, two weeks after he received his ban for his comments on the officiating against the same opposition.

Asked if Erasmus was passing on messages during the Ireland game, Springboks assistant coach Felix Jones said: "I've no idea, we were busy with a Test match."

Fellow assistant coach Mzwandile Stick added: "Maybe he was communicating with his followers on that party that he was having, but with us we were just in the game."

Build-up to the heavyweight contest at the Aviva Stadium was dominated by Erasmus' sanction, with the watch-along representing a potential breach of World Rugby's rules should Erasmus have been recorded criticising any decisions or communicating with any members of the playing or coaching staff.

Jones continued by saying the situation was not a distraction as the Springboks slipped to a second successive loss, before questions on Erasmus were quickly shut down by the team's media officer.

"Thank you for everything this week. The messages, the photos and the support mean a great deal to me," Erasmus said in a post on X on Monday.

"Losing is never nice, but we are still number one in the world and we are in the final of the Nations Cup. So let's go again.

"I'd love to watch it with you. Put the final on your own TV on Sunday and join me."

Ireland head coach Andy Farrell savoured a "big night for everyone who's Irish" and a major stepping stone in his side's journey towards next year's World Cup.

Robert Baloucoune claimed two first-half tries and Ronan Kelleher added another, with a long-range penalty from Sam Prendergast ultimately proving decisive amid a colossal defensive effort.

"It's something that we've been looking forward to and tried to challenge ourselves with about delivering when it matters against top-line sides," said Farrell.

"We knew that this fixture was coming, playing against the world's best - world's best by a stretch at this moment in time, I would have thought so.

"It was a game that we wanted to challenge ourselves and see how we went and obviously fronting up and showing the character that we did and coming out the right side of the win is a big night for everyone who's Irish."

South Africa ensured a pulsating encounter remained tantalisingly poised until the final whistle thanks to scores from Morne van den Berg and Malcolm Marx, plus seven points from the boot of Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu.

"I think we've taken a step forward and that was the aim," said Farrell.

"This game mattered to us in how we prepped for it. We didn't shy away from that and we took it on for what it was, which was a top of the tree game.

"We were able to perform. It wasn't perfect but we managed to come out with a win. The World Cup, it's all about stepping stones and this is a big one that's for sure."

Despite their defeat, South Africa progressed to the Nations Championship final at Twickenham after picking up a losing bonus point, with Ireland contesting the third-place final against Australia.

Asked about Erasmus, Farrell said: "Rassie is his own man and he's a smart guy. He does things for a reason.

"There's always going to be a plan or whatever. I don't know the ins and outs of it.

"The South African boys are in our dressing room having a beer and it's an unspoken rule that you just leave it alone, I would have thought. It is what it is."

images.caption: Image: Erasmus had questioned why multiple tackles he believed to be hip-drop challenges by France were allowed to go unpunished last time they met
Image: Ireland will face Australia in the third-place final at Allianz Stadium Twickenham
Image: Ireland's win against the World Cup winners was their fifth in six Nations Championship matches
Image: Erasmus will host his second watch-along for the Nations Championship final against France

articles.title: Lewis Moody says he 'felt ready to play' after former captain joined England to face New Zealand's Haka
articles.summary: Former England captain Lewis Moody joined England to receive the Haka ahead of their 37-12 victory over the All Blacks on Saturday; Moody fronted England's arrow-head formation for the pre-match tradition
articles.body:
Emotional scenes unfolded at Allianz Stadium, as Moody, who was diagnosed with motor neurone disease (MND) in 2025, walked arm-in-arm with Itoje onto the field.

New Zealand's players clapped as the former England captain took up position at the front of England's arrow-head formation - between Itoje and Ellis Genge - to accept the challenge of the Haka.

Moody, who won 71 international caps during his career, had presented England's players with their matchday shirts at their Pennyhill Park base on Friday, and revealed Ollie Chessum had jokingly urged him to stay on the pitch and chase down the first kick.

"I honestly felt ready to play," Moody told BBC Breakfast .

"When the lads were hugging me after the Haka, I was like: 'Right, I'm ready to go'."

"The night before, Ollie Chessum told me where they were going for the first kick-off.

"He was like: 'Mate, if you're up for it, you can chase it!'

"I was almost ready to take him up on that."

In support of Moody's Front Up to Motor Neurone Disease campaign, England's players wore boots as well as special warm-up and arrival kit with the campaign's logo printed on them.

The players also signed warm-up tops and match shirts, which were donated to the My Name'5 Doddie Foundation, a charity founded by the late Scotland international Doddie Weir that provides funds for MND research.

"I was really aware that this was something that I would never get to feel again and hadn't felt for over 15 years," Moody said.

"So, I wanted to try and fully take in the moment.

"When I got out there, Maro [Itoje] brought me out there and positioned me.

"Ellis [Genge] embraced me, the bundle of physical energy that he is. That's inspiring in itself, to feel the power that's emanating through his body.

"The noise was almost overwhelming. And then [I tried] to recentre myself and focus on the Haka, through the peripheral vision of the England team that fanned out in front of me.

"It just brought a huge smile, and brought back a lot of wonderful memories of playing with all my former team-mates."

He added: "It was really unique and I feel humbled to have been a part of it."

Front Up to MND are organising a series of coastal walk fundraisers on June 12 2027 to raise money for the My Name'5 Doddie Foundation.

"To have the response that it did and to have the support that it has is only good for the cause that I was there for, which is the Front Up campaign supporting My Name'5 Doddie Foundation, to raise as much money as possible, to have a serious impact on this disease," Moody said.

"We need more drugs that have a significant impact for patients. They are the breakthroughs that we're looking for and this campaign will get us near, if not over the line with that.

"But we need thousands, if not tens of thousands, hundreds of thousands of people to support and get involved.

"And hopefully, if you're a little bit inspired or if you just loved watching the game at the weekend, and everything that represented, and you fancied taking on a challenge, come and join us on June 12, walking the coast."

Atkinson: It was special to be a part of

Asked whether Moody's presence motivated England, Seb Atkinson told Sky Sports News:

"Definitely, he came into the hotel last night and gave us some reflections on his career and some reflections on his diagnosis.

"It was really special to be a part of that. I think the lads really took it on board.

"Then to hear the noise of him coming out and taking part in our response to the Haka was really special.

"Also to see his family and his sons and speak to himself [Moody] in the changing rooms after, it just topped it off."

articles.title: Ellie Kildunne: Bristol star responds to Harlequins time-keeping reports
articles.summary: England and Bristol Bears full-back Ellie Kildunne makes a pointed reference to reports that poor time-keeping was behind her Harlequins exit.
articles.body:
England and Bristol Bears full-back Ellie Kildunne marked her return to former club Harlequins with two tries, victory and a pointed reference to reports that her poor time-keeping was behind her Stoop exit.

Kildunne, with a watch drawn on taping around her wrist, ran in two first-half tries in a 48-21 victory at the Stoop in the first round of the PWR on Sunday.

"You've all seen the headlines. Why would I have a watch on my wrist?" the 27-year-old told TNT Sport after the match.

She later posted a photo of the watch drawing on Instagram , external with the caption: "Right on time."

Kildunne, who was not quoted in Quins' announcement of her departure in June, subsequently said she was "gutted" to be leaving and that it was "as much a shock to me as everyone else".

The Bears, who also signed Wales back row Bethan Lewis in the summer, finished eighth in the nine-team top flight last season.

Kildunne was not the only England star to enjoy success against the former club, with Tatyana Heard, who was part of big-spending Sale's summer recruitment drive, enjoying a 31-17 win over Gloucester-Hartpury.

Gloucester-Hartpury, who won the title three times in a row between 2023 and 2025, are without a head coach after Dan Murphy left on the eve of the season.

Champions Saracens and Ealing Trailfinders, who lost to Saracens in June's final, best Leicester and Loughborough Lightning respectively.

articles.title: Rugby gran MJ eyes Christmas number one with techno track
articles.summary: MJ, aged 70, is releasing her debut single to "dance and rave to" at Christmas, on Friday.
articles.body:
A 70-year-old gran is set to release her very own high-energy Christmas charity single vying to be this year's number one.

MJ, from Rugby, says her festive techno track Christmas Day Is Coming is one to "dance and rave to rather than the melody ones" and is "something different".

"I just thought to myself, 'I think we need a change', and I just started writing about Christmas and enjoying ourselves," said MJ, who records as Christmas Gran.

The £1 track is released on Friday and each sale will boost national charity Crisis that helps people experiencing homelessness.

MJ said that while the song is upbeat and a track to move to, she wants people to think about those who are "lonely, lost, and on the streets in the cold throughout the winter".

"If we can raise as much money as we, can it will help them through the coldest and darkest days of their life," she said.

"I've seen them taking food out of the bins that people have half eaten and it's just wrong.

"You wouldn't even let a dog lie on the streets on its own and they're fallen people for whatever reason; they could have lost their job or not been able to pay the mortgage or the rent."

MJ said she had "really enjoyed" creating the track and she "felt amazing" when she heard it.

Andy Kulesza, the track's producer whose best friend happens to be MJ's sister, said the single was "great".

Kulesza is is also a musician himself, having had some success as part of electronic trio A Million Sons, from Nottingham.

"I love it and hopefully the listeners will like it as well," he told BBC CWR.

"Seeing a 70-year-old great granny singing a banging techno cheesy dance song for Christmas, I thought nobody's really done that yet.

"I think nowadays with music you need something that's going to stand out and shock people, and this does that."

Kulesza said MJ has suffered significant loss in her life, but has stayed positive, funny and giving.

Turning to her future in the music industry, MJ has set her sights on doing a rap song.

"I would like to do a rap song with somebody so Stormzy if you are listening," she said. "He needs to get in touch because I've got another one coming out."
